catalog_quote: stress patterns in Tümpisa Shoshone are predictable and follow what Sapir (1930:39) called the law of alternating stresses. Basically, this means that every other mora is stressed, while intervening morae are weak or unstressed. A mora is any single vowel as well as the diphthongs ai or oi. Long vowels count as two morae ... Counting of alternating stressed morae may begin either on the first or second mora of a word, depending on a number of factors discussed below. The first stressed mora carries the strongest or primary stress; alternating morae afterwards carry secondary stress ... Typically, primary stress is on the first mora in the word, and every other mora afterwards is secondarily stressed. ... Usually, the second mora in the word (instead of the first) carries primary stress when the second syllable contains a long vowel while the first contains a short vowel ... As the last …

audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is confirmed verbatim in the held Dayley 1989 phonology chapter at the stated pages (435-438, with 439-440 material also matching the the primary-stress rule). Dayley 1989 is the 522-pp reference grammar Glottolog lists for pana1305 and contains the fullest stress treatment that exists; no phonology article, JIPA illustration or instrumental study of Panamint stress was found (CrossRef; The residual issue in this record is a matter of judgment, not documentary: Dayley's own text makes primary stress mora-counting with a hedged weight condition ('usually' second mora when V2 is long and V1 short, 'often varies'), which the record already carries in the primary-stress rule/qv=weight-sensitive (tentative) alongside classification fixed-strict; a second source (McLaughlin 1987/2006) could sharpen that but is unlikely to overturn

sources.quote: Every alternate mora is stressed. The first gets main stress in words without long vowels (diphthongs count as one mora). If the second vowel is long and the first is short, primary stress falls on the second syllable. If the final vowel should get a secondary stress according to the alternate count, it optionally receives that stress, if it does not the vowel is devoiced. (Dayley 1989:435)
